title: The Boy Soldier Who Never Finished His Book
author: Carl von Clausewitz
wiifm: Every plan you make will meet resistance you did not foresee: a supplier fails, a key person falls ill, a competitor does something irrational. Clausewitz gave that experience a name, friction, and built a whole theory around the gap between the plan on paper and the mess of reality. He also gave us the idea that war is politics carried on by other means. We follow a twelve-year-old Prussian ensign through defeat, exile, Russian snow and Waterloo, to a desk where he wrote a book he never lived to finish.

b: Carl von Clausewitz was born on 1 June 1780 in Burg, a small town near Magdeburg in Prussia. His family's claim to nobility was thin. His father had served as a lieutenant in the army of Frederick the Great and then worked as a minor tax official, and the household lived on modest means and large pride.

In 1792, aged twelve, Carl joined the Prussian army as a lance corporal and standard-bearer. The following year, still only thirteen, he was in action against the armies of revolutionary France at the siege of Mainz. Imagine a boy, barely older than a primary school pupil today, watching artillery reduce a city while grown men died around him.

The army he joined was still living in the shadow of Frederick the Great, who had died only six years earlier. It was famous across Europe for its iron drill, its precise manoeuvres and its harsh discipline. Officers came from the nobility, soldiers were often treated as machines, and many senior men believed the art of war had been perfected. The boy would live to see that confidence destroyed.

That early exposure matters for the book. Clausewitz never thought of war as a game of geometry, which was the fashion among many theorists of his time. He had seen it as a child. He knew it was fear, exhaustion, noise, rumour and blood, and his theory always kept those things in view.
ch.cap: Thirteen-year-old Clausewitz carries the colours at Mainz

b: After a few dull years in garrison, the young officer got his break. In 1801 he was admitted to the new military school in Berlin run by Gerhard von Scharnhorst, a farmer's son from Hanover who had risen by sheer ability and who believed the Prussian army had grown complacent and rigid.

Scharnhorst became the father figure Clausewitz needed. He taught that war could not be reduced to formulas, that officers should be educated to think rather than drilled to obey, and that history should be studied critically. Clausewitz graduated top of his class in 1803 and became adjutant to Prince August of Prussia.

In the same years he met Countess Marie von Brühl, a cultured, intelligent woman from a far grander family. Her mother disapproved of the penniless officer, and they waited years to marry, finally doing so in 1810. Marie would become far more than a wife. She was his intellectual partner, and in the end she would be the person who gave his book to the world.
ch.cap: Scharnhorst points at the map; young Clausewitz listens

ch.h: Jena and the shock of defeat
b: In October 1806 the Prussian army, still living on the reputation of Frederick the Great, met Napoleon at the twin battles of Jena and Auerstedt. It was annihilated in a single day. Within weeks Berlin was occupied and the kingdom was reduced to a rump. Clausewitz fought in the rearguard alongside Prince August, was captured, and spent the best part of a year as a prisoner in France.

The humiliation shaped everything he later wrote. Prussia had a fine army on paper, with excellent drill and proud traditions. It lost because Napoleon fought a different kind of war, using a whole nation's energy, moving fast, seeking the decisive battle and following it up ruthlessly. The old army was prepared for the last war.

His captivity was comfortable, as such things went for an officer of good family. He and Prince August were allowed to travel, and in 1807 they spent time at Coppet, on Lake Geneva, in the glittering circle of the writer Madame de Staël. But Clausewitz's letters to Marie from this period burn with shame and anger. He studied the French closely, admired their energy, and hated what they had done to his country.

Back in Prussia, Clausewitz joined Scharnhorst and a small group of reformers who set about rebuilding the army: promotion by merit, a proper general staff, training that encouraged initiative. He was learning something he would put at the centre of his theory. Strength is not what you look like in peacetime. It is what holds together when reality hits.
ch.cap: French columns break the Prussian line in Jena's fog

b: In 1812 the Prussian king, Frederick William the Third, under heavy pressure, agreed to supply troops to Napoleon for his invasion of Russia. For Clausewitz and about thirty other officers this was intolerable. They resigned and went to serve the Tsar, believing that true loyalty to Prussia meant fighting against Napoleon, even against their own king's wishes. The king never fully forgave him, and it cost him dearly in his later career.

In Russia, Clausewitz saw the campaign from inside. He was at Borodino, the bloodiest single day of the Napoleonic wars. He watched the Grande Armée reach Moscow, find it burning and empty, and then disintegrate on the long retreat. He was at the crossing of the Berezina, where thousands drowned or froze.

That December he helped negotiate the Convention of Tauroggen, in which the Prussian general Yorck agreed to take his corps out of Napoleon's army. It was a key step towards Prussia changing sides. Clausewitz saw first-hand how a single political decision could transform a military situation more than any battle.

Russia taught him something else too. Napoleon had won the battles and occupied the capital, and still lost. Victory on the battlefield, if it does not achieve the political purpose, is worth very little.
ch.cap: The Grande Armée staggers through snow from burning Moscow

b: Out of these campaigns came one of his most famous ideas. Everything in war is very simple, he wrote, but the simplest thing is difficult. The difficulties pile up and produce a kind of friction that nobody can imagine who has not seen war.

His illustration is a traveller who plans to cover two more stages before nightfall. On the map it is easy, four or five hours on a good road. Then he arrives at the post station and there are no fresh horses, or only poor ones. The countryside is hilly, the road is ruined, night falls, and he is glad to reach the next stop at all. Now multiply that by an army of a hundred thousand men, each of whom can be tired, wrong, frightened or lost.

Friction includes danger, physical exertion, bad information, weather and plain chance. Much of what is reported in war, he said, is contradictory, a great deal more is false, and most is uncertain. He also wrote about the fog of uncertainty in which much of war is waged. The famous phrase fog of war is a later paraphrase, but the idea is his.

The only lubricant for friction, he argued, is combat experience, and the quality he most valued in a commander was the ability to keep going through it. He called it coup d'oeil, the quick eye that sees the truth in a confused situation, together with the determination to act on it.

He was just as interested in what kind of person can lead through friction. In a famous chapter he describes military genius, not as a magical gift but as a blend of qualities. Courage in the face of danger, and courage to accept responsibility. An intellect able to see through the fog. And above all determination, the strength to hold to a decision while doubts and bad news pour in, without becoming stubborn when the facts truly change. He thought a calm, balanced temperament was worth more in war than flashes of brilliance.
ch.cap: A coach sinks in mud; the post has no horses

b: The war against Napoleon was not over. In 1813 Prussia finally changed sides and Clausewitz, still in Russian uniform, served on the staff of the allied armies. That spring his mentor Scharnhorst was wounded at the battle of Lützen, and he died of the wound in Prague that June. Clausewitz lost the man who had made him, and he spent years afterwards defending Scharnhorst's memory.

In 1814 Clausewitz was allowed back into the Prussian army, and in June 1815 he served as chief of staff of the Third Corps under General Thielmann. While Blücher led the rest of the Prussian army to join Wellington at Waterloo, Thielmann's corps held off Marshal Grouchy at Wavre, a desperate fight that kept a large French force away from the decisive battlefield.

Then came peace, and with it a career that never quite took off. In 1818 he was made director of the War College in Berlin, but it was an administrative post and he had no say over teaching. The king still distrusted him. So for twelve years he used the time differently. He sat down and wrote.

He studied over a hundred and thirty campaigns, from Gustavus Adolphus to Napoleon, and kept rewriting his thoughts on what war actually is. He had a horror of theory that told a general what to do. He wanted a theory that would educate the mind, helping a commander understand the nature of what he faced, rather than handing him rules.
ch.cap: Clausewitz rewrites On War amid towers of paper

b: The book opens with a definition. War is an act of force to compel the enemy to do our will. Then Clausewitz does something clever. He imagines war in its pure, abstract form, which he calls absolute war, in which each side keeps escalating until one is completely destroyed. And then he shows why real war almost never looks like that.

Real wars are limited by time, by friction, by uncertainty, and above all by politics. And here comes the sentence for which he is best known: war is merely the continuation of policy by other means. The word in German, Politik, covers both policy and politics. War is not an independent thing with its own logic. It is a tool, and its purpose is set by the political aim.

This has a radical consequence. The size of the effort should match the value of the political objective. A small aim justifies a small war. And the soldiers should never be allowed to run a war purely on military logic, because the war only makes sense in terms of what it is for.

He sums up the nature of war in what he called a remarkable trinity. It is made of three tendencies: primal violence, hatred and enmity, which he linked mainly to the people; the play of chance and probability, which belongs to the commander and his army; and subordination to policy as an instrument, which belongs to the government. A good theory, he said, must keep all three in balance, like an object suspended between three magnets.

In a note he wrote in 1827, Clausewitz drew a distinction he wanted to run through the whole revised book. There are two kinds of war, he wrote. In one, the aim is to overthrow the enemy, to make him politically helpless or militarily impotent. In the other, the aim is merely to seize some territory on his frontier, either to keep it or to use it as a bargaining chip at the peace table. Most wars in history were of the second kind. Napoleon had made people forget that.

From this, he drew what he called the first and most far-reaching act of judgement for any statesman and commander. They must establish what kind of war they are embarking on, neither mistaking it for something it is not, nor trying to turn it into something alien to its nature. Get that wrong, and every later decision rests on a false foundation.
ch.cap: Statesmen and generals argue; policy holds the balance

ch.h: Centre of gravity and the culminating point
b: Two more ideas from On War have travelled far beyond the army. The first is the centre of gravity. Out of the enemy's characteristics, Clausewitz argued, there develops a hub of all power and movement on which everything depends. It might be his army, his capital, his alliance or his leader. That is the point against which all your energy should be directed.

The second is the culminating point of victory. An attacker grows weaker as he advances: his supply lines lengthen, he must leave garrisons behind, and the defender falls back on his own resources. There comes a moment when the attack has used up its strength. Push beyond it and you invite a counterblow worse than anything you suffered while advancing. Napoleon in Russia was the perfect example.

Clausewitz also argued, against intuition, that defence is the stronger form of war, though it has a negative aim. The defender chooses his ground, waits, and benefits from the attacker's exhaustion. The ideal is to defend until the moment is right and then switch to a sudden, powerful counterattack, which he called the flashing sword of vengeance.

These ideas lend themselves easily to ordinary life. A business taking on a bigger rival should ask where that rival's centre of gravity lies: a key client, a brand, a single founder. A growing firm should ask whether it is approaching its own culminating point, when new offices and new staff are outrunning cash and management attention. And anyone in a dispute should remember that the side which waits on strong ground often has the advantage.
ch.cap: The advance thins out; a counterstroke flashes back

b: In 1830 Clausewitz was posted to Breslau, then to the Polish border during the uprising there, where cholera was spreading. On 16 November 1831, back in Breslau, he died suddenly, probably of cholera, at the age of fifty-one. His great book lay in sealed packets. A note he left in 1827 said he planned to revise the whole thing, and that only the first chapter of Book One was in its finished form.

Marie von Clausewitz edited the papers and published them, with a moving preface, between 1832 and 1834. So On War is an unfinished work, sometimes contradictory, and readers have argued over what he really meant ever since. In the late nineteenth century German generals quoted him to justify seeking total destruction of the enemy, often ignoring his insistence that politics must govern war.

He has had critics. Basil Liddell Hart, whom we meet later this week, blamed him for the bloodbaths of the First World War and called him the Mahdi of mass. Many scholars think that is unfair, since it confuses Clausewitz with the people who misread him. The best English translation, by Michael Howard and Peter Paret in 1976, did much to restore his reputation.

What survives is not a manual but a way of thinking. Keep the purpose in front of the method. Expect friction. Find the hub everything depends on. Know when your advance has run out of strength. And remember that the boy at Mainz learned all this the hard way.
ch.cap: At dawn, widowed Marie lays out the sealed packets

take: War is the continuation of policy by other means. In business, every tactic, campaign and fight should be judged by the goal it serves, not by its own internal logic.
Clausewitz argued the effort should fit the value of the political aim. Before escalating a dispute or a project, ask whether the prize is worth the cost.
Everything is simple, but the simplest thing is difficult. Build slack into timelines and budgets, because staff illness, bad data and small delays always pile up.
Every organisation has a hub on which everything depends. Know your own so you can protect it, and know your competitor's before you attack.
Advances weaken as they stretch. Expansion that outruns cash, people or attention invites a reversal, so stop and consolidate before you reach it.
The defender chooses ground and lets the attacker exhaust himself. Sometimes the best move is to hold a strong position and strike when the rival overreaches.
Clausewitz refused to write rules. Use frameworks to sharpen how you see a situation, not as a script to follow.
Generals misread Clausewitz to justify slaughter. Read the original before trusting what others say a thinker meant.
recall: What is friction in Clausewitz's sense?
It is the mass of small difficulties, such as danger, exhaustion, bad information, weather and chance, that make simple things hard in war. It is what separates war on paper from real war.
What does war is the continuation of policy by other means imply?
That war is a tool serving a political purpose, not an independent activity. The scale of the effort should match the value of the aim, and political leaders should govern its conduct.
What are the three parts of the remarkable trinity?

Primal violence, hatred and enmity; the play of chance and probability; and subordination to policy as an instrument. He linked them mainly to the people, the army and its commander, and the government.
What is the culminating point of victory?
The moment when an attack has used up its strength through lengthening supply lines and losses. Pushing beyond it invites a damaging counterattack, as Napoleon found in Russia.
Why is On War sometimes contradictory?
Clausewitz died of cholera in 1831 before revising it, and said only the first chapter was finished. His widow Marie published the manuscripts from 1832 to 1834.
note: Biographical details follow Peter Paret's Clausewitz and the State and the Howard and Paret translation of 1976. His service at Mainz, Jena, in Russia, at Tauroggen and at Wavre, and his death in Breslau in 1831, are documented. The phrase fog of war is a later paraphrase of his language. Liddell Hart's attack on him is widely regarded as a misreading, and scholars still debate how far the unfinished text should be read as a single coherent theory.
words: The ability to take in the true shape of a confused situation at a single glance.

stories: The widow who published the masterpiece

In November 1831 Carl von Clausewitz died suddenly in Breslau, probably of cholera, aged fifty-one. His life's work sat in sealed packets, with a note from 1827 saying he meant to revise the whole thing and that only the first chapter of Book One was finished. His wife Marie, a countess whose mother had once disapproved of the penniless officer, edited the papers and published them between 1832 and 1834 with a moving preface. So the most influential book on war in the Western tradition reached the world through a woman, and it is unfinished. That is exactly why generals and scholars have argued over what he really meant ever since.

In 1812 the Prussian king, under heavy pressure, agreed to lend troops to Napoleon for the invasion of Russia. Clausewitz and about thirty other officers found this intolerable. They resigned and joined the Tsar, reasoning that true loyalty to Prussia meant fighting Napoleon, even against their own king. Clausewitz saw Borodino, the burning of Moscow and the frozen crossing of the Berezina. That December he helped negotiate the Convention of Tauroggen, which took a Prussian corps out of Napoleon's army and helped swing Prussia to the other side. One political act changed more than a battle could. The king never fully forgave him.

Clausewitz explained friction with a traveller. Late in the day he decides to cover two more stages before nightfall. On the map it is easy: four or five hours on a good road. Then he reaches the post station and there are no fresh horses, or only poor ones. The country turns hilly, the road is ruined, night falls, and he is glad to reach the next stop at all. Now, said Clausewitz, multiply that by an army of a hundred thousand men, each of whom can be tired, wrong, frightened or lost. Everything in war is very simple, he wrote, but the simplest thing is difficult.
biz: Map your friction from click to completion

Every enquiry has a post station with no fresh horses. This week, walk one real HomeownersLoan lead and one Debt Support Direct case through every step and write down where they stall: a missed call, a WhatsApp reply that waits overnight, a lender asking twice for the same document, a debt client too anxious to open their post. Then measure two numbers weekly: time from enquiry to first contact, and drop-off between each stage. Fix the single worst stage first. For distressed clients, friction is often fear, so a shorter document list and a named contact may do more than any script.
Know your culminating point before you grow

Clausewitz warned that an advance weakens as it goes until it overreaches. A brokerage reaches that point when leads outrun the people who answer them: response times slip, callbacks are missed and customers get worse outcomes, which is a Consumer Duty problem as well as a commercial one. Set a capacity line now: the number of new enquiries per day your team can contact within your target time. Track answer rate and speed to contact against lead volume, and treat any rise in budget that pushes you past the line as a loss, not a win. Grow the team before you grow the spend.
connects: Clausewitz's friction, where small mishaps pile up beyond anyone's plan, is the military ancestor of Perrow's argument that tightly coupled systems produce failures nobody designed.
Both books start from the gap between the simple plan and the messy reality, and Gawande's checklists are one practical lubricant for the friction Clausewitz described.
Liddell Hart attacked Clausewitz as the Mahdi of mass, though most scholars think he was arguing with Clausewitz's misreaders rather than the man who said politics must govern war.
recap:
In seventeen ninety-three, a Prussian boy of thirteen stood under fire at the siege of Mainz. His name was Carl von Clausewitz, and he had joined the army at twelve. He never afterwards thought of war as neat geometry on a map. He had seen it as fear, noise, rumour and blood.

His teacher, Gerhard von Scharnhorst, taught him that officers should be educated to think, not drilled to obey. Then came the shock. In eighteen hundred and six, at Jena, Napoleon destroyed the proud Prussian army in a single day. It had looked magnificent on paper. It had been ready for the last war. Clausewitz learned that strength is not how you look in peacetime but what holds together when reality hits.

In eighteen twelve, when his king agreed to help Napoleon invade Russia, Clausewitz resigned and joined the Tsar. He watched Napoleon win battles, take Moscow, and still lose everything on the frozen road home. Victory that does not achieve the political purpose is worth very little.

After Waterloo he was given a dull desk in Berlin, and for twelve years he wrote. Out of that came the big ideas.

The first is friction. Everything in war is very simple, he wrote, but the simplest thing is difficult. Bad information, weather, exhaustion and chance pile up until the plan on paper bears little resemblance to the day itself.

The second is the famous sentence that war is the continuation of policy by other means. War is a tool, its purpose set by politics, so the size of the effort should match the value of the aim, and the first judgement of any leader is to understand what kind of war he is actually in.

The third is the centre of gravity, the hub of power on which everything else depends, where your energy should be aimed.

The fourth is the culminating point. Every advance weakens as it goes. Push past the moment your strength runs out, and you invite disaster, as Napoleon did in Russia.

And the fifth is character. He valued the quick eye that sees the truth in confusion, and the determination to hold a course without becoming stubborn when the facts truly change.

In eighteen thirty-one he died suddenly of cholera, his book unfinished in sealed packets. His wife Marie edited it and gave it to the world. Readers have argued over it ever since.

The line to remember: keep the purpose in front of the method, and expect the road to be harder than the map.
